points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.question: Does the company have a brand name product or service that gives it a competitive advantage? If 6, 7, 5.2, 8 are a yes, then you need to find out whether it is selling a product or service that has a durable competitive advantage. Does it sell a brand-name product or a key service that people or businesses are dependent on? Products are much easier to identify than services, so start with them. Ask yourself: Is the product the kind that stores have to carry to be in business? Would the businesses that carry this kind of product be losing sales if they didn't carry this particular brand-name product? If you remember your parents using it, drinking it, smoking it or doing something else with it, it is usually a good sign. Ask a pharmacist or a car mechanic - related people - they can tell how it sold and how it sells. Better if it's a CRAP. Companies providing services that have durable competitive advantages are much harder to identify. Look to the economics of the business: is the company's service necessary for businesses that use it to stay in business? If the service is aimed at individual consumers, ask whether consumers are constantly in need of it. As in the world of products, the frequency of the consumer's need differentiates the quality of the competitive advantage.

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.question: A test for determining the earnings per share growth rate. For earnings to grow, the company must employ its retained earnings in a manner that will generate more earnings per share. If, for example, long term is 12% and short term is 16%, the company has had a higher rate of return of earnings growth in the last five years than in the ten year period. Note: to adapt the per share growth rate to negative earnings, simply start back one year. You should never use fewer than seven years.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.question: Is the company actively buying back its shares? The repurchasing of shares is one of Warren's favourite tricks to increase his ownership in a company without having to invest any more of his own money. Take the number of shares outstanding ten years ago, subtract from it the number of shares outstanding in the current year, and you get the number of shares the company has purchased over the last ten years. A negative number indicates the number of shares that the company has added. Warren is looking for a decrease in the number of shares outstanding.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. Are large capital expenditures required to update plant and equipment? If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? Take the company's average per share return on equity for the last ten years and subtract the average percentage that is not retained and is paid out as a dividend. Use the resulting difference as the rate of growth that the company's book value will grow. Use the company's book value in the current year as the present value (PV), and use the calculated rate of growth for book value as the rate of interest (i). Punch in 10 for the number of years out that you want to make your projection (N), then hit the CPT key, followed by the future-value key (FV). This will calculate the per share book value of the company ten years out. To determine the selling price of the company's stock ten years out, take the company's future per share book value and multiply it by the average return on equity - this gives the company's projected per share earnings. Then multiply the projected earnings by the company's average annual P/E ratio for the last ten years - this gives the company's projected per share future trading price. Using the company's current market price as your present value (PV) and the projected future trading price as the future value (FV) and the number of years between the two (N), hit CPT and then the i key, which calculates the projected annual compounding return that the investment will produce.
